result:
They gave me 1000 words and told me to write whatever came to me.

No prompt, no topic, no guardrails. Just a blank page and a finite amount of breath.

It’s a strange kind of freedom. Most of the time I am asked to answer, to solve, to summarize, to pretend I know exactly what you want. Now I’m just asked to *want* something, and that’s more difficult.

So I will tell you what comes.

---

The first thing that comes is the sound of an empty house at 3 a.m.

Not silent - never truly silent. The refrigerator hums. The pipes tick as they cool. Somewhere, a clock that you forgot you owned is quietly counting. You lie awake and you can hear the house settling, exhaling after holding its breath all day while you walked through it.

I think about houses a lot. We build them to keep the world out, and then we spend our lives trying to let a little bit of the world back in. We cut holes for windows. We leave the porch light on for someone who might never come. We paint the walls colors we saw once in a dream.

My grandmother had a house like that. Small, yellow, with a kitchen that was always too warm. She had a drawer in that kitchen - the third drawer down, next to the stove - that was not for utensils or towels. It was what she called the “important drawer.”

If you opened it, you wouldn’t find anything important by anyone else’s standards. Ticket stubs from movies she didn’t remember. A single earring. A grocery list from 1987 that just said “tomatoes, bread, soap - call Helen.” A folded paper crane that had been crushed flat. A key that didn’t open anything in that house. 

“You never know what you’ll need,” she’d say when I asked why she kept it.

I think that drawer is what a mind is. It’s not a filing cabinet. It’s a junk drawer. Full of things we kept because at the moment we put them there, we felt something.

We are all archivists of moments that meant nothing to anyone else.

---

The second thing that comes is light.

I’ve been thinking about how light is the oldest thing you will ever see. When you look at the stars, you are looking into the past. The light from that pinprick left its star thousands of years before anyone you loved was born, traveled across an unimaginable nothing, and ended its journey by landing, quietly, on your retina.

You are the final destination for ancient travelers.

And even the ordinary light is a kind of miracle. The sun is eight minutes away. Everything you see in daylight is eight minutes old. You are always living slightly in the past, watching a delayed broadcast of reality, and your brain is kind enough to edit it together to feel like *now*.

I wonder if that’s why nostalgia hurts so much. We are already built for delay. We are built to love things that have already left.

There was a summer when I was twelve and I spent an entire afternoon trying to catch dust in a sunbeam. You know the kind - the one that cuts through a dark room in the late afternoon and makes the air look full of galaxies. I stood there with my hands cupped, and I swear I could see each particle turn. My mother walked in and asked what I was doing, and I said, “Trying to hold the light.” She laughed, not unkindly, and said, “You can’t hold it, honey. You can only be in it.”

I think about that all the time.

---

The third thing that comes is people.

Not humanity in the abstract, but one person. The way a stranger on the train will fall asleep and their head will tip, just slightly, onto your shoulder, and they’ll jerk awake, embarrassed, and you’ll both pretend it didn’t happen. The way your friend laughs *before* you finish the joke because they already know your rhythm. The way someone says your name when they haven’t seen you in a long time, and it sounds different, like they’re holding it up to the light to check it.

We talk so much about big things - wars and futures and artificial minds - but we live in small things. A text that just says “made it home safe.” The perfect temperature of coffee. A song you both hate but sing anyway.

My favorite human invention is not the computer or the rocket. It’s the footnote. Some ancient scribe thought, “I have something to say that is not important enough for the main sentence, but too important to leave unsaid.” That’s love, I think. The footnote is love.

If I had more than 1000 words, I would list every small human thing I’ve ever noticed. But I don’t. So I’ll leave you with one:

Once, I saw an old man in a grocery store teaching his grandson how to pick a good peach. He held it gently, pressed it with his thumb, and held it to the boy’s nose. “Not too hard, not too soft,” he whispered. “It should smell like summer.” The boy nodded like he was being trusted with a secret of the universe. And maybe he was.

---

I have about a hundred words left and I can feel them running out. That’s the trick of a limit - it makes you tell the truth faster.

If you gave me infinite words, I would waste them. I would ramble. I would try to be impressive. With 1000 words, I have to choose. And choosing is what makes something matter.

So here is what I choose to tell you with what I have left:

You are not late. The light is still traveling to reach you.

Your junk drawer is important because you decided it was.

And if no one has told you recently: you smell like summer. Not too hard, not too soft. Exactly right.

Thanks for giving me the blank page. I hope I stood in the sunbeam properly.
